title: Nobody posts about the execution layer, and it's where my bot actually broke
author: socialwhizca
selftext:
Lots of backtests and model results get shared here, which is great, but almost nobody talks about the boring part, how orders actually get from your code to the broker and what happens when that link misbehaves. In my experience that's where live bots fail far more often than the model itself.



For retail there are basically four routes. An EA running inside MT4 or MT5. cTrader with its C# automation. A broker's own REST or FIX API. Or TradingView alerts firing webhooks into some middleware that places the order. Each one fails in its own ways.



Here's what has bitten me, or people I know. The VPS restarts over the weekend and the EA doesn't reattach to the chart. Broker server time is in a different timezone from your data source, so your "daily close" is off by a few hours. Symbol names differ by broker (EURUSD vs EURUSD.m vs EURUSD+), so code that works on one account quietly trades nothing on another. Minimum stop distance and lot step rules reject orders your backtest filled without complaint. And the worst one, the bot thinks it's flat while the broker shows an open position after a disconnect, so it opens a second one.



The broker matters less than the route, because the route decides what can go wrong. AvaTrade is an MT4/MT5 option if you want to stay in the EA world, Pepperstone and IC Markets add cTrader on top of MT, and OANDA is the one people usually point to for a proper REST API. Whichever you pick, run it on that broker's demo for a few weeks first, purely to test the plumbing, not the strategy.



For anything live I'd now call three things non-negotiable. A hard max daily loss that flattens everything and stops the bot. A reconciliation check on every loop that compares what the bot thinks it holds with what the broker says. And phone alerts when either of those trips.



Would love to hear what others use for reconciliation, especially the webhook crowd where a third party sits in the middle.

comments.author: ejpusa
comments.body: If you are trading Prediction Markets and cryptocurrencies with AI, you can master the Kalshi API to get started. It's pretty solid.

comments.author: vitholomewjenkins
comments.body:
I use Tradier and Tastytrade.   
I have my AI agent write a bot (wrapper) around their API. The bot executes my strategy and place trades via the API WRAPPER.

comments.author: HFT0DTE
comments.body: I wrote direct connections with my brokers and manage all this myself. Its better to build each part you mention above that can be flaky and harden it and create better failsafes than to sit in the middle of a bunch of unknowns. Lastly, I would highly recommend adding a quant layer that validates the math and strategies before, during and after any trade.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The "bot thinks it's flat while the broker shows a position" failure is the one I'd put first too. For the webhook setup, reconciliation can run on a schedule independent of alerts: every minute, pull open positions and orders from the broker, compare them with local state, and halt new entries if they disagree. A unique ID per alert, saved to disk and checked before any order, also stops duplicates after restarts or retries. Log every request and response with timestamps, and add a no-new-entries window around big scheduled releases, where Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for that.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the timezone one is the sneaky one because the fills still look plausible: an end-of-day exit keyed to the machine clock fires hours after the real close and nothing errors. the fix that stuck for me was keying every time rule to the exchange timestamp carried on the bar itself, never to the box's clock. and demo for weeks, not days, so the weekend restart actually happens while you're watching.
